# Repository concepts

This document owns repository-specific design, lifecycle, and operator decisions that span files. It is not a file inventory or a replacement for the [chezmoi reference](https://www.chezmoi.io/reference/). Source files define behavior; [`AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md) owns contributor workflows and safety boundaries and routes each maintenance task here or to a narrower path rule or skill.

## Bootstrap

Bootstrap remains interactive because it crosses account-specific input, system-level installation, and hardware-backed GPG keys. Scripts provision tools and machine state that file synchronization alone cannot express.

Scripts in [`.chezmoiscripts`](../.chezmoiscripts/) use `before` and `after` attributes to place ordering dependencies around file synchronization. Within a phase chezmoi runs them by target name, and the names carry no ordering prefix: a script that needs a sibling from the same phase checks for it before writing anything, so a name that sorts wrong fails at that check on a fresh machine instead of half-configuring it. The GPG script checks for the binaries the Brewfile installer provides, the glab setup script reads the envchain namespace the seeding script fills, and the coding-agent installer provides its own Node through `proto install` because `reconcile-dev-tools` sorts after it. `run_once` and `run_onchange` encode rerun behavior using the standard semantics in [chezmoi's script guide](https://www.chezmoi.io/user-guide/use-scripts-to-perform-actions/). Neither is a health check: a script runs again only when its rendered content or target name changes, so state changed outside the source, such as a tool removed by hand, stays until the script is scheduled again. To schedule one `run_onchange` script, delete its entry with `chezmoi state delete --bucket=entryState --key="$HOME/.chezmoiscripts/<target name>"`, where the target name drops the source attributes and `.tmpl`, as `setup-gitconfig.sh` does for `run_onchange_after_setup-gitconfig.sh.tmpl`; `chezmoi status` then shows it as `R`, and the next apply runs it. `run_once` entries are keyed by content hash instead, so `chezmoi state delete-bucket --bucket=scriptState` schedules every `run_once` script at once.

Script identity includes rendered comments and other non-executable bytes. A comment-only edit to a `run_once` or `run_onchange` source can therefore schedule the script again, and a `Brewfile` comment changes the explicit hash embedded in its installer. A `run_onchange` script is keyed by its target name as well, so renaming one reschedules it with its body unchanged. Treat those comments as operational input and edit them only when the resulting rerun is in scope.

Most tools a script runs print progress or no-op notices that only matter when they fail. Run such an external command through `step` from [`.chezmoiscripts/.lib/step.zsh`](../.chezmoiscripts/.lib/step.zsh), which the script sources from `$CHEZMOI_SOURCE_DIR`: it replaces the command's output with a status line naming the command and replays the output only when the command fails, and `chezmoi apply -v` streams the output instead. A command that prints nothing when it has nothing to do needs no wrapper. A wrapped command reads `/dev/null` and by default shows nothing while it runs, so commands that need the user, such as vendor installers, `brew bundle`, sudo, browser sign-in, GUI launches, and YubiKey operations, stay unwrapped. Editing the library changes no script's content, so it reruns nothing and takes effect when each script next runs. Adopting it does change a script's content, so a script whose rerun needs the user adopts it only along with another change to that script.

These dependencies shape the sequence:

- Homebrew and [`Brewfile`](../Brewfile) packages provide tools used by later scripts.
- proto resolves every tool version from `~/.proto/.prototools`, which chezmoi writes from [`dot_proto/dot_prototools`](../dot_proto/dot_prototools) during file synchronization. The dev-tools script runs in the `after` phase so proto can read that declaration before installing runtimes and reconciling the npm, uv, and mbx tools. In the `before` phase that file does not exist yet, and proto refuses to install a tool whose required Node.js version is unconfigured.
- `claude` and `pi` come from their vendor installers in `run_once_after_install-agent-clis.sh`, and `codex` comes from the `codex` cask declared in [`Brewfile`](../Brewfile). The script runs in the `after` phase because Pi needs the Node that `~/.proto/.prototools` declares, and it sorts before `install-herdr-integrations`, which registers hooks for all three.
- launchd LaunchAgents own gpg-agent and keyboxd, and `no-autostart` in `~/.gnupg/common.conf` stops every client from starting one implicitly: a daemon started from a sandboxed agent shell keeps that sandbox for life and cannot reach the YubiKey. The GPG script writes and bootstraps those jobs in the `before` phase after Homebrew installation, because chezmoi needs the private keys while synchronizing encrypted files. It is `run_onchange` keyed on the Homebrew kegs those daemons link, so an upgrade of gnupg or of one of its libraries restarts them with the files now on disk. dirmngr is deliberately unmanaged, so keyserver operations fail explicitly instead of autostarting it; the script imports the card's public key over HTTPS from the URL stored on the card instead of using the card's `fetch` command.

A dedicated case-sensitive `Code` volume is provisioned as machine infrastructure rather than managed as a normal file target. It is unique, belongs to the APFS container that stores `$HOME`, and is mounted persistently by UUID through `vifs`. Provisioning must refuse to mount over a non-empty `~/Code` or to proceed when `~/Code` or the volume is mounted elsewhere, and must never unmount a volume automatically; a matching volume already mounted at `~/Code` is reused whatever it holds. The `run_once` script provisions fresh-machine state rather than reconciling later drift; its Python test covers deterministic logic, while APFS, Disk Arbitration, and reboot acceptance remain manual Mac checks.

This repository uses Input Source Pro's [exported JSON](../.chezmoitemplates/input-source-pro/settings.json) as the source of record instead of writing `com.runjuu.Input-Source-Pro` with `defaults`, because its app and website rules live in a Core Data store and many of its preferences are archived values. [The import script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_import-input-source-pro.sh.tmpl) first launches the app and waits for its process so the user can complete first-run Gatekeeper prompts, then dispatches `inputsourcepro://import` with the source file's path. URL imports replace settings without the GUI's confirmation and report success or failure in an app alert; `open` returning only proves URL dispatch. `.chezmoitemplates` is never deployed, so the export needs no ignore entry.

## Package and tool ownership

Where a tool is declared follows from how much update lag its owner tolerates:

- Coding agents tolerate none. `claude` and `pi` come from their vendor installers, unpinned, in one `run_once` script in the `after` phase; `claude` updates itself, while `pi` updates only when `pi update` runs, so the unattended-upgrades job invokes it. Pi keeps its managed install rather than its Homebrew formula or npm package because only the managed install pins its transitive dependencies. `codex` comes from the official `homebrew/cask` CLI cask in [`Brewfile`](../Brewfile), which moves its update onto the same job and reports `brew upgrade --cask codex` as its update action.
- Agent-adjacent CLIs (`ctx7`, `oracle`, `herdr`) also sit in `Brewfile`; `oracle` comes from `steipete/tap` because it has no self-updater. `brew bundle` has no entry type for gh extensions, so [`run_onchange_after_install-gh-extensions.sh`](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_install-gh-extensions.sh) installs `gh stack` and `gh actions-lock` at apply time, which needs no gh sign-in: Claude Code's sandbox cannot write gh's extension directory, so an agent there cannot install them on first use.
- Background development tools (`typescript`, `typescript-language-server`, Pyright, mbx) are pinned in `.github/dev-tools` and bumped by Renovate behind a release-age window.
- Runtimes (`node`, `bun`, `pnpm`, `go` through proto; Rust through rustup) resolve through their own managers, with no pin and no window. The `oracle` and `ctx7` formulae pull in Homebrew's `node` (and `pnpm` for oracle), which sits behind proto's shims on `PATH` and is not a runtime channel, so those CLIs execute a Node this repository does not pin.
- GUI and daily-use apps are `Brewfile` casks, and App Store-only apps are `mas` entries. Logseq deliberately remains outside Homebrew ownership: this machine uses manually installed 0.10.15 because 2.x is incompatible, so its cask is not a fallback path.

The Brewfile installer runs `brew bundle --no-upgrade`, so an apply only installs missing entries: the unattended-upgrades job below upgrades formulae and casks, and the App Store updates `mas` apps, automatically only while its Automatic Updates setting is on, which this repository leaves to each machine.

[`Brewfile`](../Brewfile) is the package declaration. The managed [LaunchAgent](../private_Library/private_LaunchAgents/com.liby.unattended-upgrades.plist.tmpl) runs the managed [unattended-upgrades helper](../private_Library/private_Application%20Support/com.liby.unattended-upgrades/executable_unattended-upgrades) on a 02:00/08:00/14:00/20:00 local-time calendar trigger plus `RunAtLoad = true`, which intentionally adds an immediate login or reload run. The helper has its own executable path so Login Items can name the job after its basename. [`run_onchange_after_setup-unattended-upgrades.sh.tmpl`](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-unattended-upgrades.sh.tmpl) registers the job in the user's `gui/$UID` domain after file synchronization and embeds both files' hashes so a change reloads the job; a `Brewfile` change never reloads it.

The helper runs `pi update` after `brew upgrade`, then runs `pi update --extensions` to update installed extension packages, and `gh extension upgrade --all`, because an installed gh extension only prints an upgrade notice. Those Pi steps put `~/.local/bin` on `PATH` for the managed launcher and keep the proto shims there for the Node it needs. It then runs `rustup update`, because rustup never refreshes an installed toolchain on its own, whichever channel it tracks. Once a week it also reclaims the pnpm store and metadata cache, the npm cache, and the uv cache, which none of these tools trims by itself. Both the Brewfile installer and this helper recursively clear `com.apple.quarantine` from the Codex cask after their package operation, including its code-mode and voice helpers: approval of the CLI does not approve those separate executables or carry over on upgrade. Homebrew can still prompt during installation when the cask runs `codex completion` before returning. The helper restarts gpg-agent and keyboxd when either daemon is missing or no longer reports the installed GnuPG version; a library-only upgrade leaves that version unchanged, so it is caught by the next `chezmoi apply`. The job uses its own helper rather than the `domt4/autoupdate` tap, which schedules only Homebrew commands and would drop the helper's Pi, gh extension, Rust, quarantine, GnuPG, and cache steps.

Every cask that declares `auto_updates true`, from `Brewfile` or installed by hand, is upgraded only by its own updater: [`dot_homebrew/brew.env`](../dot_homebrew/brew.env) sets `HOMEBREW_NO_UPGRADE_AUTO_UPDATES_CASKS`, which `bin/brew` loads into every brew process while `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` stays unset, so `brew upgrade` and `brew bundle` skip such casks without `--greedy` whether the job, the installer, or a shell runs them, and the cask definition rather than a repository list decides. Casks without that flag, such as `codex`, still upgrade through the job.

`Brewfile` owns the `proto` executable, while [`dot_proto/dot_prototools`](../dot_proto/dot_prototools) declares the tools and versions under `PROTO_HOME` that the dev-tools script installs; proto's standalone installer is not a fallback path. `proto upgrade` breaks that ownership in two places at once, so upgrade proto through Homebrew only. It writes `proto` and `proto-shim` into `$PROTO_HOME/bin`, which the tool shims and any shell that puts that directory first both resolve ahead of Homebrew, so later `brew upgrade` runs stop reaching the proto those callers execute. It also rewrites the directory of the running executable, because that executable sits outside proto's own inventory; under Homebrew that directory is the Cellar. Proto's own version check does not conflict with Homebrew ownership, because it only prints a notice pointing at `proto upgrade` and never installs anything; `PROTO_VERSION_CHECK=0` silences it. An alias such as `lts` or `latest` is resolved again on every `proto install`, which bypasses the remote-version cache, and on every shim invocation, which re-enters `proto run` and reads a cache refreshed every 12 hours; the Node plugin maps both aliases to exact versions, so a moved target installs on the next `proto install`, and `auto-install` installs a resolved version that is missing. `auto-clean` runs after `install`, `outdated`, `status`, `activate`, and `regen`, and removes only tracked versions whose `.last-used` marker is older than 30 days, so a version some project still runs stays installed wherever the alias now points.

The exact global npm tool versions live in [`.github/dev-tools/package.json`](dev-tools/package.json), Pyright lives in [`.github/dev-tools/requirements.txt`](dev-tools/requirements.txt), and mbx is pinned in [its release installer](dev-tools/install-mbx.sh), which checks the official release archive against the release's `SHA256SUMS` and installs it into `~/.local/bin`. Renovate groups these declarations with other dependencies, and one shared `run_onchange` installer installs the proto-declared tools and then reconciles each declaration independently without pruning unrelated machine-local tools; do not split the installer. The dev-tools workflow supplies their status check; a file-scoped Renovate `ignoreTests` must not be restored because it can become branch-level configuration on a mixed dependency group. `typescript`, `typescript-language-server`, and Pyright back Claude Code's LSP plugins, which [`.chezmoitemplates/claude/settings.json`](../.chezmoitemplates/claude/settings.json) enables; `typescript-language-server` falls back to the global `typescript` when a workspace's own cannot provide tsserver.

Each of these declarations carries a release-age cooldown, so a compromised upstream release has time to be reported and yanked before it is pinned here. npm and PyPI enforce it twice, and the two halves are coupled: the installer refuses to resolve an artifact younger than its window, so the matching Renovate rule in [`.github/renovate.json`](renovate.json) has to wait at least as long or it pins a version the installer cannot reach. [`dot_config/uv/uv.toml`](../dot_config/uv/uv.toml) sets the PyPI window through uv's `exclude-newer`, and the installer renders the same value into its own `uv tool install` command rather than relying on uv discovering the deployed file. The installer sets the npm window through `npm config set`, which writes it to `~/.npmrc`; an environment variable set in `.zshenv` would miss npm processes that do not inherit that environment. `~/.npmrc` also carries registry tokens, so the source declares the setting through the command rather than tracking the file. The GitHub release rule is mbx's only window, because its installer fetches the exact pinned release. All windows are the same value, and one value is enough because the declarations hold only background tools that nobody waits on.

mbx is the machine's Cargo build cache. `mbx setup` installs a `cargo` shim that [`dot_zshenv`](../dot_zshenv) puts ahead of `~/.cargo/bin`, so every plain Cargo command, an agent's included, shares one store of compiled outputs. Each stored output is keyed on the complete rustc version and is never reused by another toolchain, and the unattended-upgrades job replaces a bare `nightly` every day, so keep rustup's default on stable, which moves on a six-week cycle; a project that needs nightly pins a dated one in its `rust-toolchain.toml`. The dev-tools installer puts the store, managed targets included, under `~/Code/.mbx`, on the volume that holds the checkouts. A checkout's default `target` becomes a symlink to a managed directory that mbx removes when the checkout disappears, goes unused, or exceeds the disk budget, and mbx keeps the link out of `git status` through `.git/info/exclude`. Projects and agent instructions therefore need no mbx-specific steps. A target chosen through `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, `--target-dir`, or `build.target-dir` stays unmanaged, so a project should keep Cargo's default location. Changing `cache_dir` on an existing machine requires explicit migration: mbx does not copy the old store, and collection only scans the configured root. When a build result looks stale, rebuild with `MBX_VERIFY=1` in a fresh target directory, which compiles beside the cache and compares the outputs; Cargo compiles nothing it considers up to date, so a plain rerun compares nothing.

[`.chezmoiexternal.toml`](../.chezmoiexternal.toml) pins the zsh plugin archives at fixed commits. The GitHub archive manager in [`.github/renovate.json`](renovate.json) updates those commits from each declared branch.

## Repository validation

GitHub discovers workflow YAML only directly under [`.github/workflows`](workflows/), so keep that directory flat. Checks cheap and deterministic enough to run on every change are jobs in the unfiltered [`validate-repository`](workflows/validate-repository.yml) workflow; a check gets its own path-filtered file only when it is slow or depends on the network. Keep behavior tests beside their owner when chezmoi ignores the test filename; reserve [`.github/tests`](tests/) for repository-only tests that cannot safely live beside a managed source. Bun tests there use the `*.test.ts` name and run through `bun test ./.github/tests/`; Python tests use the conventional `test_*.py` name that `unittest discover` finds there; add a concern subdirectory only when multiple tests benefit from that grouping.

A check derives its expectation from the source that owns the contract, such as a parsed configuration, an include list, frontmatter, or the list a script itself declares, or it states a requirement that source must meet, such as the tools a hook must cover. Do not copy a file's current values, wording, or command help into a test as its expected value: such a test fails on behavior-preserving edits and protects nothing the copied file does not already state. Add a check only for a realistic edit whose failure would otherwise surface after it is merged and applied, or never, such as an automerged Renovate pin or a hook that stops running; a removed flag or a missing credential that the next call reports needs none. The repository deliberately leaves these unvalidated:

- Installed CLI behavior. Homebrew upgrades the CLIs that skills call several times a day, independently of this repository, so a check that runs when a skill changes runs at the wrong time. Verify a skill's CLI syntax against the installed version when editing it; an adopted skill follows the upstream tag recorded in its `metadata`.
- Runtime enforcement of skill frontmatter. The [skill registry test](../dot_agents/skills/skills.test.ts) checks that Claude Code, Codex, and Pi load each skill with its name and description intact and that every frontmatter key is one Claude Code documents; whether a runtime honors a field's value, such as Claude Code's auto mode dropping interpreter grants from `allowed-tools`, needs a check in that runtime. Codex's skill catalog budget counts every installed skill, not only this repository's; past it, Codex shortens every listed description, user skills included, without a warning.
- Credential-path policy for tool calls, which the [agent guard](#agent-guard) package owns and tests. The review skill's path classifier covers only the changed paths whose bodies a diff would print, which the guard cannot see.
- The content of instruction and documentation prose, such as which routes `AGENTS.md` lists or whether text restated for another reader, like the auto-mode scope entry, still matches its source. A test cannot tell a deliberate rewrite or removal from a mistake, so the diff review owns it.
- Template rendering. The scoped `chezmoi diff` before each commit renders every changed target on the machine that applies it, so a CI render would need its own synthetic data and catch nothing that diff misses.
- Anything that needs the Keychain, the YubiKey, a signed-in account, or a fresh machine, such as `guard-bash` running before Homebrew has installed the guard; those stay manual checks on the Mac.

Every path-filtered workflow lists itself, the tests or validator it runs, and the production sources that can change the result. When a non-required workflow filters both `pull_request` and `push`, use a [YAML anchor](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/reusing-workflow-configurations#yaml-anchors-and-aliases) for the identical path lists. GitHub leaves the required check for a [workflow skipped by pull-request path filters](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/troubleshooting-required-status-checks#handling-skipped-but-required-checks) pending, so before making one required, trigger it for every pull request and move any filtering below the workflow level. Reference each action by its version tag and let [`actions.lock`](workflows/actions.lock) lock it to a commit: run `gh actions-lock` after adding a workflow or changing a `uses` reference, since GitHub enforces the lockfile only for the workflows it lists. Renovate regenerates the lockfile with its own action updates, so its configuration pins no digests, which the lockfile would replace again. Keep `permissions` read-only, disable checkout credential persistence, cancel superseded runs for the same ref, and give every job a finite timeout. Extract a reusable workflow only for a complete job shared by multiple callers, or a composite action for a meaningful repeated step sequence; do not hide isolated fields or one checkout step behind an abstraction.

The `validate-repository` workflow runs for every pull request and every push to `main`, so its checks have no path list that a rename can leave stale, and it can become required without a path-filter skip deadlock.

## Configuration ownership

Most source files and templates render to paths under `$HOME`. Standard source names and template mechanics follow chezmoi rather than repository-specific conventions.

Not every configuration is fully replaced. Applications such as Codex and Claude Code write mutable runtime state, so [`modify_` sources](https://www.chezmoi.io/reference/target-types/#modify-file) manage selected fields while preserving application-owned values.

Replace subtrees that source fully owns so that removed fields disappear from the destination. For shared subtrees, preserve application-owned fields through an overlay or explicit exceptions during replacement. Establish ownership from the application's writers rather than the shape of the configuration. An overlay preserves undeclared fields; removing a source declaration does not by itself retire its destination state.

Deleting a source file likewise leaves its existing destination in place, and `chezmoi status` no longer reports that unmanaged path. The repository avoids persistent deletion lists and migration markers so source describes the current configuration without accumulating past removals. The trade-off is that existing machines need explicit cleanup; `.chezmoiremove` would automate file deletion but not cleanup of fields in shared configurations.

The JSON and TOML modifiers compare parsed values before serializing, so reordering object keys in their fragments alone leaves the destination unchanged. Fragments embedded in scripts, such as [`codex/requirements.toml`](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/requirements.toml), also affect script trigger hashes; their ordering changes can rerun the consuming script.

Chezmoi source manages portable, durable preferences, including established interaction habits, when they should remain consistent across machines. It leaves matching convenience defaults implicit unless an explicit value enforces a repository boundary or counters observed write-back drift. Generated runtime state, machine-specific paths, and settings synchronized elsewhere remain owned by their existing systems.

The [macOS defaults script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-macos-defaults.sh.tmpl) owns the Apple UI preferences. Its whole-array writes replace a list wholesale, so a tile dragged into the Dock, a stack, or an input source added by hand does not survive a rerun, and its input source, language, and appearance values take effect at the next login rather than in the running session. Each key's own reason stays in that script's adjacent comment. The [app setup script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-apps.sh) owns the third-party app preferences written with `defaults`, with each key's reason likewise in its adjacent comment, and registers login items through System Events, which writes the database the Login Items pane shows rather than a preference domain. A single fixed archived value, such as Xnip's shortcut, is written by that script as data; an app that stores many archived values and offers a readable export, such as Input Source Pro, is imported from that export instead.

### Shell startup

A login shell reads [`~/.zshenv`](../dot_zshenv), `/etc/zprofile`, [`~/.zprofile`](../dot_zprofile), and, when interactive, `/etc/zshrc` and [`~/.zshrc`](../dot_zshrc), in that order. Ghostty tabs, Herdr panes, and VS Code's integrated terminal are login interactive shells, and so is the shell VS Code starts to read its environment when opened from the Dock. Codex and Claude Code start each session by capturing a login shell that also sources `~/.zshrc`, then run every command in `zsh -c` with part of that state restored: Codex restores its exported variables, Claude Code only its PATH, functions, aliases, and options. Without a snapshot they run the command in a non-interactive login shell, which skips `~/.zshrc`. chezmoi's shell scripts are `#!/bin/zsh` and read only `~/.zshenv`. Pi's `bash -c` and the launchd helper read no zsh file and use the PATH they inherit or set. Exports that any zsh needs and the toolchain directories that must precede Homebrew therefore belong in `~/.zshenv`. Homebrew's and OrbStack's environment, and the PATH order that `/etc/zprofile`'s `path_helper` disturbs, belong in `~/.zprofile`, which ends by putting the toolchain back in front. `~/.zshrc` holds what only an interactive shell uses, such as completion, history, aliases, plugins, proto's per-directory activation, and the prompt.

### Codex configuration

[`.chezmoitemplates/codex/config.toml`](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/config.toml) declares the source-owned portion of `~/.codex/config.toml`. The modifier replaces `plugins`, `permissions.development`, and each source-declared `mcp_servers` table, carrying forward only the destination's existing `node_repl.env` and `node_repl.env_vars` within those server tables. All other declared configuration is deep-overlaid. Replacing server tables removes stale transport fields that can make Codex reject the whole configuration. Removing an entire server from source still requires explicit destination cleanup. While `default_permissions` is set, every apply also deletes `sandbox_mode` and `sandbox_workspace_write`, because those legacy selectors can override the profile; that enforced absence is current configuration, not a record of a past removal.

Leave `model`, `model_reasoning_effort`, and per-app authorization out of source (its `apps.*` tables declare only each app's `enabled` flag) so changes made in Desktop, the TUI, or the live file survive an apply. [Herdr integrations](#herdr-integrations) owns `features.hooks`. Desktop generates `node_repl` environment fields and can later replace its runtime tables, so an apply does not prevent subsequent application write-backs. Do not declare the legacy standalone `mcp_servers.computer-use` registration in source: source declarations can override the same-named plugin registration and conflict with [Desktop-owned runtime state](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/24387#issuecomment-4531286877). Keep the bundled `computer-use` and `unified-computer-use` plugins enabled; `unified-computer-use` provides Desktop's `cua_repl` browser and computer runtime. Keep the bundled `code-review` plugin disabled: it adds a second GitHub path for pull-request comments and merges beside the `gh` and `review` skills.

Desktop persists registered preferences under `[desktop]` and removes their legacy global-state or persisted-atom copies after migration. Manage a registered preference in [`.chezmoitemplates/codex/config.toml`](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/config.toml); reserve the global-state fragment for current persisted atoms that have no registered Desktop setting.

`~/.codex/.codex-global-state.json` is also partially managed. [`dot_codex/modify_dot_codex-global-state.json`](../dot_codex/modify_dot_codex-global-state.json) overlays [the portable global-state fragment](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/global-state.json), which keeps Mini's closed state, onboarding completion, dismissed announcements, active-line Git blame, Work home composer mode, and explicit review diff filter (`branch`) portable; every other global-state entry remains Desktop-owned. These keys belong to the current Desktop implementation rather than the public `config.toml` schema, so verify the installed app before changing or expanding their managed paths. A running Desktop process can overwrite an external apply with its in-memory persisted-atom values, so change these preferences through the UI or apply this target while Desktop is stopped.

Keep `approval_policy = "on-request"`, `approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"`, and the sole custom `default_permissions = "development"` profile together. [`.chezmoitemplates/codex/requirements.toml`](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/requirements.toml) constrains that tuple because Desktop builds a new task's approval policy and reviewer from its saved agent mode rather than from `config.toml` ([#33552](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/33552)): unconstrained, the saved `auto` mode yields `on-request` / `user` and `full-access` yields `never` / `user`. The constraint intentionally removes the built-in modes, including Full Access. Restart Desktop after changing that file: no reproduction has yet shown Desktop hot-reloading an edited `requirements.toml`. The [Browser modifier](../dot_codex/browser/modify_config.toml) deliberately overrides that posture for the Browser tool, granting no-prompt full-CDP control so an agent run is not gated on a human at the keyboard; the modifier owns the exact keys, values, and their invalidation condition.

The same requirements file registers [`guard-bash`](../dot_codex/managed-hooks/executable_guard-bash) from `~/.codex/managed-hooks` as the one `PreToolUse` Bash hook, and it hands each event to the shared [agent guard](#agent-guard).

The same requirements file enables a second managed hook, [`contextual-markdown-links`](../dot_codex/managed-hooks/executable_contextual-markdown-links), on `UserPromptSubmit`. It injects the Markdown link-placement instruction as `additionalContext` on every prompt because Codex ignores `UserPromptSubmit` matchers and the same context must cover links discovered after tool calls.

The [Codex requirements script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-codex-requirements.sh.tmpl) installs the rendered requirements as root-owned `/etc/codex/requirements.toml` because Codex ignores requirements in an unforced user preference such as a `defaults write`. The script needs sudo, so apply it from an interactive terminal.

The `development` filesystem profile remains standalone with `:root = write`, `~/.ssh` denied except the exact `config`, `allowed_signers`, and `known_hosts` entries that ssh and Git signature verification use, exact read-only `.env` and `.env.local` entries under every workspace root, and no copied per-tool cache lists or broad command allows. Programs may consume credential and environment files through their normal interfaces; changing or deleting one still requires the user's explicit request. Filesystem capability does not authorize remote Git or secret-bearing chezmoi operations.

[openai/codex#40254](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/40254) tracks the current macOS reproduction in which Chrome fails trusted RPC path validation without an explicit Browser cache read rule. Keep `~/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-bundled/browser` as the only extra read-only path so the trusted worker can load Desktop's runtime-owned Browser service; a chezmoi `private_` or `readonly_` source and `chmod` do not create a trusted permission root. Remove the exception only after deleting the source rule, applying the rendered configuration, fully restarting Desktop, confirming the effective permission table no longer contains the rule, and succeeding on the first Chrome initialization in a fresh task without a prior Browser attempt or retry.

Keep `features.network_proxy = false` with `permissions.development.network.enabled = true` so public and local networking remain direct while the filesystem profile stays enforced. Add proxy-only `domains` or `allow_local_binding` only when managed proxy enforcement exists; [openai/codex#33227](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/33227) documents the unresolved proxy-only local binding failure.

Both `cli_auth_credentials_store` and `mcp_oauth_credentials_store` stay on explicit `keyring`; `auto` may fall back to plaintext files. Before activating this on another machine, use a credential-safe status check against the exact store to confirm the existing login. Agents never migrate, rewrite, or delete the real store.

`features.daemon_auto_start = false` keeps Codex from starting a shared app-server daemon, so each TUI runs its own embedded app server. A shared daemon runs every attached session's hooks and tool commands with the environment of the terminal that first started it, so Herdr records sessions on the wrong pane or on none, and `HERDR_*` inside tool commands names a pane the agent is not in ([herdrdev/herdr#4649](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr/issues/4649), [openai/codex#48500](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/48500)). A TUI still attaches to a daemon that is already running, such as one started before the setting was applied, and stopping that daemon leaves its TUIs offline rather than moving them to embedded servers. To retire it, wait until none of its sessions is working, quit each attached TUI and keep the `codex resume <id>` it prints, run `codex app-server daemon stop`, and resume each session in the pane it came from; the session's next turn runs the hook that reports that pane to Herdr again. `codex queue` does not need the daemon and still reaches a busy embedded session.

### GitLab CLI configuration

glab reads its configuration from `~/.config/glab-cli`, which [`dot_zshenv`](../dot_zshenv) selects with `GLAB_CONFIG_DIR` instead of the macOS default under `~/Library/Application Support`, because Claude Code's sandbox can write `~/.config` but not `~/Library`. glab writes its sign-in state into that `config.yml`, so the [config modifier](../dot_config/private_glab-cli/modify_private_config.yml) sets only the top-level preferences it declares, on every apply, and leaves the rest to glab. The [glab setup script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-glab.sh.tmpl) copies the private host's OAuth application ID from envchain with `glab config set` and runs glab's web sign-in only when glab has never signed in to that host.

Sign-in stores the tokens in that `config.yml` in plaintext instead of glab's default Keychain storage. glab must save new tokens at every refresh and refuses to refresh where it cannot, and Codex cannot run glab where the Keychain is writable: its sandbox denies the shared-memory write that a Keychain write makes, and while its profile denies `~/.ssh`, escalation cannot move a command out of that sandbox. Keychain storage would therefore cost the `~/.ssh` protection, yet it never kept the tokens from agents, which read them through glab inside their sandboxes; what plaintext gives up is the protection of copies of the file, such as backups. Each refresh invalidates the previous tokens, so a copy is useful only until the next refresh, unless a thief refreshes first and keeps the session; glab's next refresh then fails with `invalid_grant`. Sign in again with the setup script's login line: the bare `glab auth login` that `glab auth status` suggests puts the tokens back in the Keychain.

### Claude Code configuration

[`.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md`](../.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md) is the path-scoped owner for Claude Code settings, sandbox, integration, and runtime-state decisions. Its path frontmatter makes Claude Code load it only for the matching sources; other Agents must follow the route in [`AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md) before changing those sources.

### Pi configuration

`~/.pi/agent/models.json` and `~/.pi/agent/keybindings.json` are fully managed, while `~/.pi/agent/settings.json` is partially managed. The [settings modifier](../private_dot_pi/private_agent/modify_private_settings.json) replaces each top-level key declared in the [settings fragment](../.chezmoitemplates/pi/settings.json), including the entire `modelThinkingLevels` map, and preserves undeclared keys. Applies intentionally overwrite UI-saved startup and per-model defaults so devices share the source configuration.

Temporary `/model` and `/thinking` selections remain available. After applying settings, use `/reload`, then select the model again with `/model` to activate the thinking defaults; resuming a session can restore its recorded model and thinking level. `defaultProjectTrust = "always"` intentionally lets every directory load project-local settings, resources, packages, and extensions without a trust prompt.

Authenticating the built-in `anthropic` provider exposes every Claude model in Pi's catalog, and `models.json` can only add or override models on a built-in provider, not hide the rest. `enabledModels` therefore keeps `/model` and model cycling to `rc-gateway/**` and the `anthropic` models in `modelOverrides`; update both lists together when adding or retiring a Claude model, and start a new session (`/new` or a new `pi` process) to apply a scope change because `/reload` does not re-resolve `enabledModels`. `rc-gateway/**` uses `**` because Pi matches globs against `provider/modelId` with `minimatch`, where `*` stops at `/`, and the gateway's model IDs contain a `vendor/model` slash.

`defaultTools = ["+codemode"]` adds the built-in scripting tool to Pi's default tools without requiring an MCP server. Scripts can call classifier models through `models.classify()`; classifiers such as TypeSafe's Jev do not appear in the chat-model picker. The TypeSafe provider entry overrides only authentication, preserving Pi's built-in classifier catalog and System One protocol adapter.

`thinkingLevelMap` declares which thinking levels a model exposes, not preferred defaults. `rc-gateway` fronts Vercel AI Gateway, so derive the map from the entry with the same id under `vercel` in the [models.dev catalog](https://models.dev/api.json) rather than by probing, because an HTTP 200 does not prove the requested effort was honored ([gateway mappings](https://vercel.com/docs/ai-gateway/models-and-providers/reasoning#how-reasoning-is-mapped), [Fireworks API](https://docs.fireworks.ai/api-reference/post-chatcompletions)). Each value listed in the entry's `effort` reasoning option is the value for the Pi level of the same name, and `none` is the value for `off`. Write `null` for a standard level (`off`/`minimal`/`low`/`medium`/`high`) the entry does not list, and omit an extended level (`xhigh`/`max`) it does not list: an omitted standard level falls back to the provider's default mapping while an omitted extended level stays unsupported. Do not alias levels (`minimal` to `low`, or `xhigh` to `max`), and keep preferred defaults in `settings.json`.

`contextWindow` in [`private_models.json.tmpl`](../private_dot_pi/private_agent/private_models.json.tmpl) is this repository's working budget, not the window the route advertises. Pi compacts once the estimated context exceeds `contextWindow - reserveTokens`, checked before each request, and caps each request's output at the room left in the budget, so changing it moves the trigger and shrinks output space together. Default to 400000 so sessions compact before long-context quality degrades, within what the route accepts. Where the vendor bills the whole request at a higher rate past a prompt-size threshold (OpenAI 272K), size the budget so the trigger falls below it; the estimate is not a hard cap, so a request can still cross. Skip that when even the higher rate is cheap, because compacting early would discard context to save little. Set `maxTokens` to the smallest of `contextWindow`, the vendor's exact documented output limit (the integer its API reference gives, not a rounded "K"), and any cap the route actually enforces; a cap a catalog only advertises, such as `max_tokens` from the gateway's `GET /api/v1/models` or models.dev's `limit.output`, is not one; DeepSeek returned more than the 32768 the gateway advertised. Use `contextWindow` when the vendor documents no output limit. `compaction.reserveTokens` is 50000 rather than Pi's default 16384 because it also sets the summarization output budget (`0.8 * reserveTokens`): the default 13107 truncated once a session's merged summary and tracked-file list outgrew it. The reserve is global, so keep every `contextWindow` well above it or give the model a `compaction.modelOverrides["provider/modelId"]` entry; a reserve at or above the window makes the trigger non-positive and compacts after every tool batch. `pi --list-models rc-gateway` shows the loaded window and output limit but cannot validate `thinkingLevelMap`.

The `rc-gateway` provider sends a Codex CLI `User-Agent` because the gateway serves `/api/v1/responses`, which the `openai-responses` models use, only to that client and rejects Pi's own; the chat-completions models ignore the header.

The [Pi extensions package](https://github.com/Entwining/pi-extensions) owns the editor, footer, guard adapter, and reasoning workaround, including their tests and releases. [`run_onchange_after_install-pi-extensions.sh`](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_install-pi-extensions.sh) installs that Git package after the CLI installer and leaves package registration to Pi, preserving other installed packages and their resource filters.

Pi's `npmCommand` exempts the `@earendil-works/*` scope from npm's release-age filter during package installation and updates. npm exempts only the packages a pattern matches, not their dependencies, and each Pi release pins sibling packages such as `pi-agent-core` from the same release, so the exemption must cover the scope rather than name `pi-coding-agent` and `pi-tui`. Third-party dependencies keep the machine's three-day window. Git package installation still resolves omitted development dependencies, so the extensions package checks its pins with the same window and exemption.

Credentials, sessions, installed packages, and recorded trust decisions under `~/.pi/agent` remain runtime-owned, so the directory must never be adopted wholesale. Both managed source directories stay `private_` to preserve mode `0700`. The gateway base URL comes from `.private.rcGatewayBaseUrl`; the rendered model file uses credential commands with the namespaces defined by the [credential consumer contract](#credential-backed-features), rather than carrying secrets.

### Oracle configuration

Oracle reads `~/.oracle/config.json`, and its `oracle bridge client` command rewrites that whole file as plain JSON with `browser.remoteHost`, `browser.remoteToken`, and `browser.remoteViaSshReverseTunnel`. The [config modifier](../private_dot_oracle/modify_private_config.json) therefore sets only its own `browser` keys and preserves the rest; a full-file replacement would delete Oracle-owned bridge state on the next apply. A config key applies only to runs that omit its flag: the [oracle skill](../dot_agents/skills/oracle/SKILL.md) passes `--browser-model-strategy`, so `modelStrategy` governs only hand-run `oracle`, while `noFocus` keeps skill runs as well from bringing Chrome to the front. The deployed file can hold a plaintext token written by Oracle's bridge, so treat it as credential-bearing regardless of its visible contents, and inspect the overlay source instead of reading, diffing, or re-adding the destination.

## Herdr integrations

[`run_onchange_after_install-herdr-integrations.sh.tmpl`](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_install-herdr-integrations.sh.tmpl) installs the Pi, Claude Code, and Codex integrations so each agent reports its native session ID to Herdr and a restarted Herdr server resumes the pane in its previous conversation instead of a bare shell. Herdr owns every file it writes, and `herdr integration status` lists them; the surprising one is `features.hooks` inside the otherwise managed `~/.codex/config.toml`. Leave that key out of [`.chezmoitemplates/codex/config.toml`](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/config.toml). The installer owns the flag's name, having already migrated `codex_hooks` to `hooks` and deleted the retired key, so a source declaration would restore what a later migration removes. Omitting it costs nothing: the modifier compares parsed values, so the installed flag survives an apply and the flush-left line the installer writes never surfaces as drift. The rendered `herdr --version` in the script is the only refresh signal, because Herdr reports outdated integrations from `herdr update`, which a Homebrew upgrade bypasses. The Claude `SessionStart` registration is the one entry that must live in source because the settings modifier replaces the whole `hooks` key; [`.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md`](../.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md) owns its required form. The Codex hook reads its pane and Herdr socket from the environment of the process that runs it, which is why [Codex configuration](#codex-configuration) keeps Codex TUIs off a shared app-server daemon.

## Agent guard

[`Brewfile`](../Brewfile) installs the [agent-guard package](https://github.com/Entwining/agent-guard) from `Entwining/tap`, providing `/opt/homebrew/bin/agent-guard`. The [Claude Code settings](../.chezmoitemplates/claude/settings.json) register that executable for Bash and file tools. [Codex requirements](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/requirements.toml) keep the hook under `managed_dir`; [`guard-bash`](../dot_codex/managed-hooks/executable_guard-bash) checks the Homebrew binary and execs it with `--runtime codex`. The guard adapter in the [Pi extensions package](https://github.com/Entwining/pi-extensions#extensions) maps Pi's tool calls to guard events and invokes the same executable.

The guard reports its own failures, including overrunning its internal deadline, as exit 2, which every runtime treats as a block. A guard that cannot start or a hook that outlives its timeout is up to the runtime: the Pi extension blocks any result other than a clean pass, and the Claude hooks set `onFailure: "block"` because Claude Code would otherwise run the call. Codex runs the call in those cases and has no such setting, so `guard-bash` blocks a missing binary itself and its hook timeout must stay above the guard's deadline.

The package owns guard rules, parser, and tests. This repository owns [`dot_ignore`](../dot_ignore): its `/Library/` entry keeps broad searches above that tree from enumerating it.

## Shared agent instructions

Global behavior shared by Claude Code, Codex, and Pi lives in the ordered fragments under [`.chezmoitemplates/agents/`](../.chezmoitemplates/agents/). Each fragment owns its section heading, and every root includes each fragment once in the same order. Only the Claude root may append runtime-specific paragraphs; the Codex and Pi roots are assembled from the fragments alone, which the agent-instruction contract test enforces. Do not put a shared heading in a root or copy a shared paragraph there. Keep coding principles in their own fragment so evaluation can remove that rendered section without changing the remaining bytes. Rendered evaluation documents are derived evidence and do not belong in this repository.

Pi consumes the shared core through [`~/.pi/agent/AGENTS.md`](../private_dot_pi/private_agent/private_AGENTS.md.tmpl), not `APPEND_SYSTEM.md`. The file's `private_` source attribute keeps the rendered instruction file owner-readable only, matching the already-private agent directory. A project `.pi/APPEND_SYSTEM.md` replaces the global file of the same name, while global and project context files coexist in Pi's project context; using the context-file path preserves the global core when a project adds its own instructions.

## Snowflake CLI execution

Every agent runs the installed Homebrew `snow` through [`~/.local/bin/snow`](../dot_local/bin/executable_snow), a Python script run by Homebrew snow's own interpreter that makes the connector's token-cache factory choose its Linux file cache, `~/.cache/snowflake/credential_cache_v1.json`. One browser sign-in then serves every later `snow` process until the token expires. The cost is the connector's Linux one: until then the token sits in a file that any process running as the user can read, so agents treat that file as a credential store and do not read it. The alternatives cost more: the Keychain asks for approval again in every concurrent process after each Homebrew Python upgrade, and turning the cache off opens a browser sign-in for every invocation.

The wrapper works only while it shadows Homebrew's `snow` on PATH. [Shell startup](#shell-startup) keeps `~/.local/bin` ahead of `/opt/homebrew/bin` in every zsh; wherever Homebrew's `snow` wins, sign-ins and Keychain prompts return. Connector 5 caches through its Rust core and has no such factory, so the wrapper fails at import once an upgrade brings it in, and the token store has to be chosen again.

The wrapper opens the sign-in page through macOS's background opener. On Claude, `permissions.allow` and `sandbox.excludedCommands` run a direct `snow` call outside the sandbox, so that opener works. On Codex, the profile's `~/.ssh` read deny holds every command, `snow` included, in the inner sandbox. There `snow` still writes the token cache through the profile's `:root` write but cannot launch a browser, so Codex's `SNOWFLAKE_AUTH_FORCE_SERVER=true` keeps the connector's loopback callback waiting while the personal `snow` skill opens the printed URL through browser control, which needs an identity-provider session in that browser. Snowflake RBAC owns server authorization. Do not narrow the route to `snow sql -q` or restore workspace `uvx` runtimes.

## Managed skill registry

[`dot_agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`](../dot_agents/skills/) is the canonical source layout for chezmoi-managed skills and is mirrored into `~/.agents/skills`; Claude Code reads that mirror through the managed `~/.claude/skills` symlink, so never add a skill under `~/.claude/skills` directly. Resolve an installed path with `chezmoi source-path` and edit the source, not the deployed copy. Exclude unmanaged installed skills from bulk maintenance, change one only when the user names it, adopt one only when explicitly requested, and leave `~/.agents/.skill-lock.json` as runtime-owned install state. Supporting `references`, `scripts`, and `assets` stay inside their owning skill; the registry has no index, manifest, or category directories.

A skill adopted from a third-party source records under `metadata` the upstream tag it was last compared with and upstream's tree at that tag; adopt only the changes the CLI behavior actually requires, and treat that upstream text as a release-matched reference for current syntax, not permission to overwrite this repository's routing, authorization, or recovery policy. A `gh skill update` that writes replaces the skill directory with upstream's, and `glab skills update` does the same with glab's bundled copy, so never run either on an adopted skill; a GitHub-hosted one also records its tag as `github-pinned`, which makes `gh skill update` skip it with a notice. The unattended-upgrades job upgrades a CLI silently, so [every `chezmoi apply`](../.chezmoiscripts/run_after_check-skill-versions.sh.tmpl) reports a skill whose recorded tag differs from the installed version of the same-named Homebrew formula. Then compare the recorded tree with upstream's at the installed tag, read from the skill directory's entry in the listing of its parent path at that tag: its `sha` in GitHub's contents API, or its `id` in GitLab's repository tree API. When the tree changed, port upstream's diff between the two tags; either way, move the recorded tag, pin, and tree to the installed tag so the report clears. For a GitHub-hosted skill without a same-named formula, `gh skill update <name> --all --unpin --dry-run --dir dot_agents/skills` checks it on demand against the latest release, or the default branch when the repository has none, and writes nothing.

The registry deliberately does not:

- Sync an adopted skill by update, merge, or overwrite; a person ports each change.
- Prove that a skill matches its CLI: upstream's skill tree is the only signal, so a behavior change or new capability upstream leaves out of its skill goes unreported, possibly with no failing call ever exposing it.
- Report between applies or hold a CLI back: the unattended-upgrades job only logs, so a CLI can run ahead of its skill until the next `chezmoi apply`.
- Track a skill whose CLI is not a same-named Homebrew formula, or a release Homebrew has not installed.

In Claude Code's `auto` mode, a skill's `allowed-tools` skips classifier review during that skill's turn for the concrete non-interpreter CLI prefixes and tools its contract owns, while cross-turn or standing host grants live in `~/.claude/settings.json` (see [`.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md`](../.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md)) and open-ended or interpreter commands stay on the sandbox and classifier path. If Claude denies a matching skill grant, preserve the contract and add the narrowest effective runtime exception backed by a reproducer.

## Identity and encrypted data

[`.chezmoi.toml.tmpl`](../.chezmoi.toml.tmpl) defines prompts for account-specific template values. Each user supplies their own values during `init`; a fork should first review which fields still apply.

Encrypted files use GPG, with private keys stored on a YubiKey. Repository-only encrypted data can seed envchain namespaces in the macOS Keychain instead of deploying credentials as ordinary dotfiles. Adapting the full repository therefore requires replacing or removing its GPG recipients and personal encrypted data.

Agents may read the top-level `~/.ssh` client config (`config`, `config.*`), public keys, `allowed_signers`, and `known_hosts` files, and nothing else under that directory. The [agent guard](#agent-guard) and Claude's sandbox enforce that list by directory, so private keys deployed there need no naming convention and no per-key rule. The Codex sandbox reopens only the exact files ssh and Git signature verification need, because its read entries take exact paths or a trailing `/**` while git-style globs (`*`, `?`, `[`, `]`) are accepted only for deny; public keys stay unreadable inside that sandbox.

### Git identity and signing

Both forges verify commits signed by the YubiKey, in different formats. GitHub verifies OpenPGP signatures from the card's signature key. GitLab verifies SSH signatures from the card's authentication key against that key as registered on the GitLab account, so the work address never becomes a user ID on the personal OpenPGP key: nothing about the employer is published with that key or has to be revoked from it later. Local Git verifies those signatures against the encrypted `~/.ssh/allowed_signers` instead, which GitLab never reads. [`run_onchange_after_setup-gitconfig.sh.tmpl`](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-gitconfig.sh.tmpl) reads the key id from `gpg --card-status` and installs [`github.config`](../.chezmoitemplates/git/github.config) with it and [`gitlab.config`](../.chezmoitemplates/git/gitlab.config) with the exported authentication key in Git's `key::` form into `~/.config/git/`, so signing reads no file under `~/.ssh`; `dot_config/git/config.tmpl` includes the GitHub file everywhere and the GitLab file for repositories under `~/Code/GitLab/`. The script derives the key itself on every rerun because the GPG script reruns on a Homebrew keg change rather than a card change. Neither script reruns when a YubiKey holding a different key replaces the card, so after such a swap schedule both, `setup-gpg-agent.sh` to import the new card's public key and `setup-gitconfig.sh` to rewrite the signing keys, as [Bootstrap](#bootstrap) describes.

[`git-ssh-gpg-agent`](../dot_config/git/executable_git-ssh-gpg-agent) exists because gpg-agent serves the card's SSH key on `~/.gnupg/S.gpg-agent.ssh` while shells keep the macOS ssh-agent in `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`. The wrapper points `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` at the gpg-agent socket, then runs `ssh` for `core.sshCommand --transport` or `ssh-keygen` as `gpg.ssh.program`, so SSH signing reaches the YubiKey from any shell, including sandboxed agent shells that inherit no agent environment. Git over SSH does too, except in Claude Code's macOS sandbox, which lets no SSH connection out: it sets `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, which overrides `core.sshCommand`, to a proxy command that cannot authenticate to its proxy. `dot_config/git/config.tmpl` therefore rewrites both forges' `git@` remotes to HTTPS for fetches and pushes alike, authenticated through `gh` and `glab`, so pushing, and fetching a non-public repository, fails while that forge's CLI is signed out. Keeping pushes on SSH would protect nothing while those CLIs' tokens can write to both forges from inside the sandboxes. Bare `ssh` keeps the macOS agent and file keys, except on `github.com` and `gitlab.*` hosts, where `IdentityAgent` names the gpg-agent socket so the card's authentication key is reachable without Git. Changing that socket means updating that entry, the wrapper, and the socket allowances in [Claude Code's sandbox](../.chezmoitemplates/claude/settings.json) and [the Codex permission profile](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/config.toml).

### Credential-backed features

The [seeding script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_seed-envchain.sh.tmpl) reads `.secrets/seed.asc` and stores each entry in the macOS Keychain through envchain. Its plaintext is TOML with one top-level table per namespace and one environment variable per single-line string value; numeric and boolean-looking values remain quoted. The template below is the machine-checked contract for entries consumed by files in this repository; other seed entries are not repository requirements.

```toml
[claude-gateway]
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN = "replace-with-value"
ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_BASE_URL = "replace-with-value"
ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID = "replace-with-value"
CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_VERTEX_AUTH = "1"
CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX = "1"

[context7]
CONTEXT7_API_KEY = "replace-with-value"

[glab]
GITLAB_CLIENT_ID = "replace-with-value"

[pi]
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = "replace-with-value"
RC_GATEWAY_API_KEY = "replace-with-value"

[typesafe]
TYPESAFE_API_KEY = "replace-with-value"
```

Each namespace's consumers:

- `claude-gateway`: The [Claude launcher](../dot_local/share/claude-launcher/bin/executable_claude) injects the `claude-gateway` namespace only in gateway mode and otherwise unsets every variable the contract above declares for it, whatever set them, so a `claude` started inside a gateway session follows the persisted mode unless its own flag says otherwise. It is an executable on `PATH` ahead of the native install in `~/.local/bin`, rather than a shell function, so the persisted mode also applies when Pi's bash, a wrapper such as `timeout`, or a script's subprocess runs `claude`.
- `context7`: Every Context7 consumer goes through the [Context7 skill](../dot_agents/skills/context7/SKILL.md), which runs the `ctx7` CLI in `envchain context7` so `CONTEXT7_API_KEY` reaches only the CLI child process. The namespace may also carry an optional `CONTEXT7_BASE_URL`, absent by default; point it, with no trailing slash, at a trusted reverse proxy that forwards the official `/api/v2` query API, and add that host to Claude Code's [sandbox `allowedDomains`](../.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md#sandbox). The global `--base-url` reaches query-mode requests, but upstream supports custom deployments only for MCP HTTP setup and treats on-premise query mode as unsupported. Validate a Context7 change by running a resolve-and-query through the skill.
- `glab`: The [glab setup script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-glab.sh.tmpl) copies `GITLAB_CLIENT_ID`, the private GitLab's OAuth application ID under the variable name glab itself reads, from the `glab` namespace into glab's configuration.
- `pi` and `typesafe`: The [Pi model configuration](../private_dot_pi/private_agent/private_models.json.tmpl) reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `RC_GATEWAY_API_KEY` from the `pi` namespace and `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from the `typesafe` namespace. The [Jev skill](../dot_agents/skills/jev/SKILL.md) runs user-approved local TypeSafe experiments through `envchain typesafe`.

The [agent instruction contract test](tests/agent-instructions.test.ts) parses the TOML block and checks that each key is named by a consumer its entry above links and that each linked consumer names one of the entry's keys, without reading the encrypted seed.
